utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, the 25th of June [as interpreted], 2010 -- January. I would like to greet everyone in the courtroom. I would like to greet the members of the OTP as well as Mr. Kruger and Mr. Stringer. I would also like to greet the usher and everyone helping us in this courtroom. We are going to complete today the questions coming from other accused after the examination-in-chief which is being done by the Defence team of General Petkovic. Counsel Nozica, you have actually used 38 minutes so far, and I was wondering how many more minutes you're planning to use.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom. I do believe that I'll be able to get through my examination in 30 minutes, at the most; 20 minutes, more likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, I have thought about the questions that were asked to you -- that were put to you, and I have also looked into your answers, and, therefore, I would like to put to you the following question, and I would like you to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know you left the HVO in August in order to join the Croatian Army, and then you went for some training, but I've been asking myself why you actually left the HVO while there is actually a conflict, so to say. This person has a high-ranking position within military intelligence because he is the personal adviser of the head of the VOS, so why is he leaving? And until now, I haven't really found an answer to this question, so I will give you some ideas and you can perhaps tell me which one is the correct one. I thought to myself that since you were working in the intelligence area, you may have realised that the battle was lost, given that there was a major offensive from the ABiH and, therefore, hopes were rather slim, and under those circumstances you decide to leave. That was the first possibility. Second possibility: I thought that perhaps, like other officers, you did not share the political and military access of the HVO, and therefore you decided to leave. In fact, we were shown a document last week of another officer who resigned and left the HVO, so that could be another reason, another possibility. The third possibility: You were not happy with the work you were doing, because I should like to remind you that originally you were more into technical activities, given that you followed the course in the Faculty of Mechanics, and therefore military intelligence was not really your main area of competence and, therefore, you left. But there could be other reasons as well; family reasons, romantic reasons. What led you to leave your position and join the Croat Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I mentioned that already earlier on. It was for purely family reasons. Upon completion of my education in Zagreb, had I gone back with my wife and child - on the 2nd of September, 1994, in actual fact, a child was born to me - and when I went home, my sister would be left without a room to sleep in. Now, when I finished my schooling in Zagreb, I reported to the Personnel Department of the Ministry of Defence of Herceg-Bosna, and at the time the head of the Personnel Department was Mr. Stojic here present, Mr. Bruno Stojic over there, and he sent me on to Mr. Stipo Maric, who at that time dealt with problems of accommodation, housing problems. And they weren't able to provide me with a flat for my wife and child. When that was not feasible, then I sent in a request to Zagreb, and they solved my housing problem. I was put up in Cavtat, in a hotel for displaced persons, and so I lived with my wife and child and worked in Dubrovnik. So those are the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Indeed, last week you touched upon this issue, but you did not give us those details. You said that you went to see Mr. Stojic, and you looked at the situation, and he sent you to speak to Mr. Stipo Maric. And then you say that there was no accommodation. I'm rather surprised. If I look at the case of the Prosecutor and the documents that were put to us, it was possible to actually get apartments that had been left empty by Serbs who had fled. And for those who are interested, according to the doctrine, there were about 40.000 Serbs who would have left Bosnia-Herzegovina during that time to go back to Serbia, which means that quite a lot of apartments were freed or left empty. And despite all this, you said that there was no accommodation, which means that in Mostar and the entire surrounding areas, all flats were occupied. And given that you had a wife who was pregnant, because I believe that she gave birth in September 1994, you were not in a position to get a bigger accommodation. You were living in a flat with your sister, so there were issues, and this is why you left. So you confirm that in August 1993, there were no free accommodations for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's right, they weren't able to provide me with adequate housing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, that's clear. Counsel Nozica, please go ahead. Well, I will give the floor to the counsel, who will proceed with the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too, Mr. Jasak.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd first of all like to say that as far as I've been told, Mr. Stojic's monitor is not working, so could the Technical Service see to that. Secondly, may I just for a moment go back to Judge Antonetti's question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I didn't understand you wholly. Maybe it's my mistake. Did you go to see Mr. Stojic in August 1993, as it says on page 4, line 16 -- lines 15 and 16, or did you go to see him when he was in the Personnel Department in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's how I understood you. But in response to Judge Antonetti's question, who asked you, Was it in 1993, you answered in the affirmative. So I just wanted to put that right, and that's been done. We needn't go back to that. Mr. Jasak, on Thursday, the 21st of January, I showed you five documents dealing with plans of the BH Army for military operations from Konjic to Neum and Ploce, and the last document was 1D1210. These documents dated to the period of February and September 1993, and what I'd like to ask you now -- I hope you have the binder. Do you have my binder with those documents? It's the pink binder. Yes, that's it. Can we look at the last document on that topic, which is 2D257. And just tell me when you've found it, please.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, this is a letter dated the 7th of October, 1992. The letter is signed by Zejnil. Through your operative work, Mr. Jasak, did you know who Zejnil was, the commander of Tactical Group 1 from Konjic? Did you know his surname?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that it was Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. That is the man. And he's writing a letter to the president, and from the contents of the letter we can see that that is Mr. Izetbegovic. Now, in the letter he describes the military situation at the beginning of the counter-offensive of the Serb forces in the territory from Hadzici, Igman, Trnovo and further on. I'm speaking slowly to give you a chance to read through the whole letter, although I'm just going to refer to a portion of it. So if need be, you can read through the whole letter. Anyway, what I'd like to focus on is the part linked to my examination, and I'd like to draw your attention to the last sentence on the first Croatian page, which is paragraph 3 in the English. And Mr. Zenic [as interpreted] says as follows: "We have all the conditions necessary to -- for the functioning and securing of the Supreme Command. And at this point in time, it would boost morale. And if no weapons are coming in, we could nonetheless solve the manpower problem and, in a short period of time, create a free territory. Gorazde, Foca, Kalinovik, Hadzici, Konjic, Nevesinje, Stolac, and access to Neum." Now, the next sentence is not very precise, but I think that we can glean what it is about: "This is our only solution to get out of the independence of Croatia so that we can continue to progress." Now, this word, "neovisnost" is questionable, whether Mr. Zejnil actually wrote that and meant that, but my question to you is as follows: Does this document show that the BH Army already in 1992, because we see the letter dated October, when there was joint combat going on, the BH Army fighting together with the HVO against the Serb Army, that they were preparing plans like this against the HVO? Does this document show that? And looking at the documents from that period or from later on, can you confirm that there were, indeed, such plans in existence?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this document we can see that the plans did exist already at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, the third topic and my final topic is the implementation of these actions by the BH Army with HVO combatants who were of Muslim ethnicity. And for us to do that, let's look at document 4D35, which is the next document. It is an order from Mr. Bajro Pizovic, the commander of the 42nd Mountain Brigade of the 4th Corps, dated the 18th of April, 1993. In the preamble to this order, Mr. Pizovic refers to an order from the 4th Corps, as we can see, 4th Corps Command, of the 17th of April, 1993. And for the record, I'm just going to say that it is document P1929. It's an exhibit. We don't have to look at it now. But, Mr. Jasak, do you know this commander, Mr. Pizovic, and do you know in what area this unit was active?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him personally, I don't know the commander personally, but I do know that he was a commander within the 4th Corps and that he was the commander of the 42nd Mountain Brigade, and that he was active south or south-east of Mostar; towards Stolac, that general area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, this document is already an exhibit, so I won't dwell on the details of it, but I'd just like to remind you that during the examination-in-chief you said that you had information according to which the BH Army did have plans to include members of the HVO of Muslim ethnicity in operations south of Mostar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, in this document, point 1 of it, it refers to positions, various positions. No, it would be 2.1, and it refers to the positions of the BH Army in the area of Rotimlje, which is a position facing the Serbs. Is that right, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the area of Stolac facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in points 2 and 3, second and third bullet point, it talks about taking positions facing the HVO in the direction of Capljina and Stolac. Is that right, judging by the places mentioned here, Buna, Gubavica, Stanojevici village, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, in the document we see further assignments, if we go on to the next page, the following assignments are mentioned. It says: "What should be done for this to be implemented?" And I'm going to read a portion of this order to you. It is to be found on page 2 of both the Croatian and the English. In the Croatian, it is in paragraph 5, and it says: "The Organ for Morale and the IPD and the military police will draft --" No, my mistake, sorry, my mistake. "VP" is religious affairs, yes, religious affairs, "VP," "Vjerska pitanja": " ... will draft a plan for informing the personnel, the members of the brigade, the inhabitants of Mostar, Capljina, and Stolac municipalities, and the Muslim soldiers in the HVO units in these municipalities. When drafting the plan, exchange views and proposals with the municipal boards of the SDA and, if necessary, in agreement with other institutions of Muslims in the territory." Now, Mr. Jasak, from this document can we see that the BH Army, and the political leadership of the Muslims, and the SDA party and other Muslim institutions, planned attack operations against the HVO with fighters in the HVO who were of Muslim extraction? And according to your information, did they actually carry this out in this area, too?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we can see quite obviously that -- well, we can see who was for information and political activities and so on and that they did this in co-operation with the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at another document, 2D286, dealing with the same topic. This document is already in evidence. This is a diary written by Safet Nozic. Let's look at the second page of the document and the entry made on the 18th of April, 1993. Let me remind you that the previous document bore the same date. Look at the entry made at 10.30, where it says "Bregava." "We will engage if a fight is imposed on us by the HVO, linking our men with the HVO-ABiH, bridge in Zito." Mr. Jasak, could you please tell us what bridge is referred to as Zito, why this name?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zito is a local name for Zitomislic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm reading on: "Check-point Buna-Blagoje-Domanovici, Stanojevici, Hodbina, forces on alert." And now it says: "Task: Bridge Zito. Check-point, Buna-Blagoje-Domanovici, Tasovcici-Capljina Bridge," an illegible bridge, "maximum safety in village." And, finally: "Taking of Stolac with our people from the HVO." Mr. Jasak, were you informed about those events? Does this document confirm what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have information about such activities. Such activities were contained in the orders by the commander of the 4th Corps of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now the last document about the same topic, 4D36. This is a report by the 4th Corps commander, Mr. Arif Pasalic, dated 2nd May 1993. And in this report, he speaks about the previous events, the events that were described by the two previous documents. In this document, I'm going to read the portion below bullet point 3, paragraph 2, and it says: "In the order that was issued to the battalion commanders and the Command of the 42nd Mountain Brigade, at a meeting held on the 17th of April, 1993, at 2200 hours: "The commander of the 43rd Brigade told us as follows:" Just let me remind you, Mr. Jasak, who was the commander of the 42nd Mountain Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the commander of the 42nd Brigade was Bajro Kvezovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I am referring you to bullet point 2, where it says: "Linking up with our men in the HVO was carried out." Mr. Jasak, does it arise from this document that in that area, before the 30th of June and before the 9th of May, 1993, there was, indeed, linking up with "our men," as it is said here, in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It transpires very clearly from this that that activity had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now it says -- since this is an exhibit, I'm not going to read everything: "The following were seized with small forces, a bridge in [indiscernible]." Is that the goal that was shown in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reference in that document was to Zito Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Further on, let me not read everything, it says: "Positions towards Domanovic, positions towards Stanojevic village," which is also mentioned in the previous document; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And let's move on to the next page. I would like to point out two more things which are relevant for this topic. Sometime on the second page, in paragraph 3, it says: "Men from the Capljina HVO have the task of taking Tasovcici village and the bridge in Capljina in order to prevent troops being brought from the direction of Metkovic." And it also says further on: "Taking the town of Stolac with our men in the HVO." Mr. Jasak, do the three documents that I've just shown you, and especially the last one, confirm the operative data that you had at the time about the plans and actions of the BiH Army; namely, to take the area together with the Muslim members of the HVO? And the area in question is the area south of Mostar, as you said it yourself.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this absolutely confirms that our assessments were correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Jasak, could you tell us about those assessments? What kind of assessments are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the assessments and predictions that the BiH Army would undertake everything possible in order to link up Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar, and everything south of that area, and also that they would use Muslims in the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jasak. I have no further questions. Your Honours, this brings my cross-examination to an end. I thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Jasak, I have a question regarding the same document; namely, number 3 on the first page. The document speaks of an ultimatum received from the 1st HVO Knez Domagoj Brigade to leave Gubavica village. I wonder whether you know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what that is about, but I know that at that time we entered the areas of responsibility of the 1st Brigade around Stolac. I don't know whether this is what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Since this is a follow-up on my cross-examination, just for the sake of clarity, maybe the witness could tell us who the 1st Brigade belonged to and which territory it entered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Brigade of the HVO belonged to the Operative Zone South-East Herzegovina, which means that I was talking about the entrances of the 42nd Brigade into the area of responsibility of the 1st Brigade, and that misunderstandings may have arisen from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now turn to the other Defence teams. 5D, 6D, I believe you don't have any questions, but I would just like you to confirm this. 5D, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, last week we already stated that we would not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 6D.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Jasak, good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're distributing the Prosecutor's binders now. There are three binders, but this is only because I've tried to divide my topics up into bite-sized sections, and each binder relates to a specific section. Your Honour, for that purpose we're distributing only binder 1. We'll distribute binders 2 and 3 during the break, but now we'll only be focusing on binder number 1. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, but before Mr. Kruger begins, we entirely understand the practical reasons for the way he proposed to deal with it, but, as a matter of fact, we would particularly request having the binders now, binders 2 and 3, because we wish to get going on working on them in various ways. So I'm sure there would be no resistance to that request. Thank you, and thank you, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's no objection, Your Honour. There was no reason except we were trying to save some time, but we understand fully the position of the Defence on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasak, just turning very briefly to a topic you were dealing with right -- a few moments ago with Defence counsel for Mr. Stojic, and there's just one thing that I'd like to clarify with you which I don't quite understand. You say or you said that regarding the area south of Mostar, you were aware that there was talk of linking up of Muslims within the HVO with the ABiH, and that this would be to the detriment or with a view to fighting or taking aggressive actions against the HVO. Do you confirm that you possessed such information?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we were privy to a piece of intelligence that what was meant was to use soldiers of the HVO who were of Muslim ethnicity against the HVO. We have already spoken about that at great length. That's the information that we had, although our commanders would not come to terms with that being possible because those men had been with them from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So I did understand you correctly. And I also understand from what you said now that this is information that you did pass on to your superiors. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, even though this relates to the area south of Mostar, if we look at the area north of Mostar, certainly, the same could very likely have been possible for the north of Mostar, that there may have been a linking up of the ABiH with Muslims within the HVO north of Mostar; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does it mean when you say "north of Mostar"? Only in the HVO units from Mostar to Capljina and Stolac, we had a large number of Muslims. North of Mostar is Bijelo Polje, so that also referred to Bijelo Polje. That was a battalion from the 2nd Brigade, the 1st Battalion. That's where there was a large number of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. So if you refer to the area south of Mostar, would that mean that HVO units which were stationed at the North Camp would be included in your concept that there was a recruitment of Muslims within the HVO? And I'm referring then specifically to the units based at the North Camp.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The 2nd Brigade of the HVO had its headquarters in the North Camp, and the 1st Battalion, Bijelo Polje, the 2nd Battalion, Mostar, and the 5th Battalion, Ilici, were parts of that brigade, the 2nd Brigade. And the 2nd Brigade was headquartered in the North Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, it is correct to say that before the attack on the 30th of June, you had warned your superiors -- you had notified your superiors of the distinct risk that there was as a result of the Muslims within the HVO? You don't deny that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying that we did provide our superiors with information that there was, indeed, such a possibility. However, our superiors made their own checks, and they talked to the commanders of those brigades, and they arrived at a conclusion that those men were performing their tasks. And the commanders thought that there would be no problems with those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And they took absolutely no measures to prepare for any eventuality or problem regarding Muslims within the HVO ranks?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, nothing was done. We were told to monitor the situation, and they told us that everything was well in check in the field, that the tasks were being performed jointly, and that positions were being held facing the positions of the VRS, which was our common enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, let's -- we'll come back to this topic at a later stage, but first off let's look at your personal details a little bit more closely. Mr. Jasak, when did you finish your schooling, in what year?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What schooling do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Before you went to the Technical -- did you say technical college to study Engineering? So your first 12 years of schooling, when would you have finished that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed the first 12 years of schooling in 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you subject to compulsory military service after that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was subject to compulsory military service in 1996 [as interpreted] and 1997 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, 1996 and 1997 or --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, 1986 and 1987. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In what area or what part of the armed forces did you do your national service?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I served in the infantry, the land army infantry, and anti-armour unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where were you based?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was based in Kosovo, in Djakovica. The commander of the brigade was Dragoljub Ojdanic, and he was headquartered in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What courses did you do, if any? Or, rather, let me put it this way: Did you obtain any rank while you were doing your military service?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the army as a private first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So you did no officer training or non-commissioned officer training?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Right. Now, sir, when you left the army in 1987, was that towards the end of 1987?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in July or August 1987. And after that, I enrolled at the School of Engineering in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: During the period between the time you left or you completed your compulsory military service, and between the time when -- or let's say before 1992, rather, were you at any stage a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Which party?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. But when?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1990, or perhaps the end of 1989 and the beginning of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you perform any specific function for the HDZ party at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a technical secretary in the party for a while in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what does that mean, that you were a technical secretary?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the municipal organisation of Mostar, I was tasked with performing the so-called technical duties, which meant that I drafted documents, maintained contacts with other branches, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In this regard, let's have a look at a document. Now, sir, if I can quickly explain to you how the binder in front of you works. You'll see that you have tabs next to -- at the side of the binder, and these tabs, even though the numbers don't follow upon each other like 1, 2, 3, they may follow like this: 400, 1.213, and so forth, so they are in chronological number order. I want you to have a look -- turn to document P11189, and that should be towards the end of your binder. It's the fifth-last document in your binder. Now, you'll see that the first document will be the English translation, and I think you'll be interested in the second page, which is the B/C/S version. And you have that in front of you. Now, sir, if we look at this document, first of all, is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And just above your signature, it says "Radmilo Jasak," and then "T, Tadjnik" or "Tajnik." What does that mean? That's secretary, but what does the T stand for?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technical secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is, indeed, a document -- you were sending out documents like these, but in your own name, during the time you were technical secretary?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And in regard to this document, I see it's marked "Very Urgent," and it says that: "You are requested to send us copies of the following documents of your municipal assembly as soon as possible." And then it says "1" and "2," but after those two numbers it says: "We need these decisions urgently so that we can complete the constitution and functioning of the Mostar Municipal Assembly in the most efficient way." Sir, you were asked during your evidence-in-chief regarding your experience of municipal assemblies, but being involved with this, did you have insight into the functioning of the Mostar Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in the functioning of the Mostar municipality. You can see that this was the collection of paper. One of our MPs, who was a member of the municipality of Mostar, simply wanted to see how communal activities should be organised. And the HDZ from Sarajevo was asked to provide them with information as to how that was done in Sarajevo, and then similar things were probably covered by the paperwork in Mostar. I never participated in the work of the municipality. I was not an MP, and I never took part in the functioning of the municipal bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you ever resign from the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not resign, I did not submit any resignations. However, since 1991, I have not been involved in any activities by the HDZ. I believe that it was sometime towards the end of 1991 when I stopped functioning as a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies. Sir, did you remain -- or you were aware of the political goals of the HDZ in 1990/1991?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you knew also about the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. However, I knew what its goals were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you, yourself, were also in favour or you supported those goals?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, let's very briefly look at just two documents. P00401, that's the first document in your binder. Now, sir, this document is dated the 22nd of August, 1992, and it's a list by the HVO Mostar Municipal Headquarters, of the headquarter staff, and it shows the units with their commanders. And all that I want to confirm with you is: If you look at number 11, it says: "4th Battalion," and then in the column for commander, it says: "Radmilo Jasak." That's you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And your deputy --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not an updated document, because by then I was already in the Main Staff. I had been the commander of the 4th Battalion, but up to the 1st of October. I'm sure that the document just wasn't updated. The information was taken over from some previous period. I'm sorry. August, August, yes, that's correct. August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And your deputy was Drago Misic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, only one further document I want to show you about this particular period, and that would be at the second-last document in your binder, 3D00671. Do you have the document? Now, sir, this is not a hugely important issue, but I'd just like to touch upon it. This is a document dated the 8th of July, 1992, and it's a report. And in this report, if we look, and this is in the second page of the English version, right at the end of that page, and unfortunately I don't have the exact reference in the B/C/S, but it's the paragraph which says: "In the 4th Battalion there is a disagreement ..." I'll read it to you: "In the 4th Battalion, there is a disagreement between the commander, Radmilo Jasak, and the chief of battalion, Bevanda, Zoran, which is --"

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my learned friend, but this is the first time that we're seeing this document in the courtroom, and I can see that it's a document from the 3D Defence. However, the document hasn't got a stamp, it isn't signed, and it doesn't even contain the name of the person who allegedly compiled it or typed it. So we don't know who the document is addressed to, it doesn't have an archive stamp or anything of that kind, so I am questioning the authenticity of the document. And can the Prosecutor provide us with some information about it? But if the witness is looking at this document for the first time, then I think that we need to settle these issues as a matter of priority. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, could you please tell us where this document comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And if I may just quickly respond to the objection, Your Honour, that the issues requested by the counsel for Mr. Coric, these are actually matters, Your Honour, which the Prosecution would deal with at length if we were to submit this document. I simply wish to put one single three-line paragraph to the witness to obtain his reaction on this. And on the basis of that, it may not even be necessary to tender the document, Your Honour. That's the sole purpose for tendering this. And as to where it came from, we did, indeed, obtain it from the 3D Defence, Your Honour, so that's where the document does come from. If I may proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this document admitted by the Chamber or not? Because I don't have a recollection as to whether this document was submitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, it has not been admitted thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, I simply want to ask you about this one little piece of information: "In the 4th Battalion, there is a disagreement between the commander, Radmilo Jasak, and the chief of battalion, Bevanda, Zoran, which is so visible that they scheduled meetings of the battalion in different places." Did this, indeed, happen? Did you and the chief of your battalion have a dispute, and it was to such -- a dispute to such an extent that you were working at cross-purposes to each other?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to what it says here, the dispute, the battalion didn't have a staff at all. And from the document we can see that my deputy was Drago Misic. Now, to convene meetings of any kind, and we mentioned this earlier on, meant that they were able to rally the troops, call a meeting, and then the commander would turn up, tell them what it was all about, and they would move on. That's what the organisation was like. But I don't know what this actually means here. That was the situation on the ground. The units were in the various districts. So in the units, we would have brothers, people who were related, or in squads, whatever, people knew each other, and if they weren't clear on something, then they would discuss the matter and organise themselves that way. So I don't know what this refers to specifically. I don't remember any people coming in for any talks or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you know any Bevanda, Zoran at that stage?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him. I knew him then, and I know him to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you have a dispute with him at that stage?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to be enlightened on the difference between "commander" and "chief." Maybe it's again a linguistic problem, but I cannot understand that there is a commander and someone different who is the chief. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Battalions had commanders, so the number-one man in command of the battalion. And he had his deputy, and that's what it says here in this document, the one that the Prosecutor showed, when we saw that that was, in fact, Drago Misic and not this other man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm afraid you -- maybe this is a linguistic problem. Here it says "disagreement between the commander and chief of battalion," and I would like you to tell me what is the difference between a commander and the chief. For me, I always thought the commander is the chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't clarify this because, Your Honour, a battalion doesn't have a chief. So it's obvious that somebody who wasn't professional compiled this document, if he can say that a battalion has a chief. A battalion had a commander and deputy commander, that's all. So we can see, if we look at the previous document, who those people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, from being a battalion commander in 1992, you then went, in October, to the Main Staff, and specifically to the Intelligence Section of the Main Staff. The first thing I'd like to know is: How did it come that you made this move? Did somebody ask you, or how did it come about?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October 1992, that's when I moved. And already before that, I got to know Mr. Keza, I met Mr. Keza. And on the basis of an exchange of information, I was invited to work with him. And, on the other hand, there was some pressure, saying that the father of Tihomir Misic would like to come in to the position of battalion commander. So the two things were linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At that stage, did General Petkovic have anything to do with your transition to the Intelligence Service?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think General Petkovic had anything to do with that, but that was -- that that was a good proposal or looking at the hierarchy, the chain of the command, the proposal came from VOS, and then the document was signed by the Defence Department. Now, whether General Petkovic had anything to do with that in the meantime, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And Brigadier Keza, how did he find you or how did he identify you so that he could recruit you?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Brigadier Keza is concerned, he, along with General Praljak, was one of the rare people who at that time early on in 1992, during very heavy fighting, came to the Command of the 4th Battalion, came to its headquarters, and that was located under Hum Hill itself. There was shelling on a daily basis around the headquarters, because it was in Tihomir Misic's house, the command and headquarters were in Tihomir Misic's house. And since we held a long line from above Ilic towards Orahovac, Hum, and so on, right up to the Old Bridge, the information which we would gather on the ground was then sent on via certain individuals who were near Brigadier Keza. They conveyed them to him, and he was satisfied with the information, and obviously he thought that I should be one of his men, one of the people who would help him in his future work and who was well acquainted with Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You were in the right place at the right time for this job, basically?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the fact that you were a member of the HDZ political party and that you adhered to or supported the ideals of a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that was probably also relevant in your recruitment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, it had no effect whatsoever, because in 1992, when I was commander of the battalion, at no meeting -- well, I didn't take part in any meeting dealing with the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your answer. I think we may have been talking at cross-purposes. My question was: The fact that you supported the ideals of a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna propounded by your political party, certainly that played a role in your recruitment. If you hadn't supported those goals, you wouldn't have been recruited to that position, would you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I make a slight objection here. I don't mind the question, as such, in principle, but I think that beforehand we should clarify something. Which ideals of Herceg-Bosna are concerned? Because there could be a great deal of misunderstanding between the witness and the Prosecutor along those lines. So the witness can give an affirmative or a negative answer without really understanding what the Prosecutor is getting at. And, secondly, if we're talking about the reactions of other people to the witness's possible support of the ideals of Herceg-Bosna, we should also lay the foundations and say how these other people decided upon his appointments or proposals and knew about any ideals that the witness supported or didn't support.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add one more sentence, because I endorse what my colleague said in objecting. This is a classical school example of speculation, a speculative question which is not in order. There are two conditionals in the final sentence, so it's not a question that the witness can answer, put like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, perhaps you can ask your question again in a clearer manner in order to obtain a clear answer to a clear question, which would avoid further objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, you have previously told us that as a member of the Croatian -- of the HDZ political party, you were aware of the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I remember, but that I didn't take part in that. So I wasn't a member of the party at the time, an active party member, and I did not take part in that, but I did know what the goals and objectives of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were. That meant to preserve the lives of everybody, wherever there were Croats and other people living with them, to become included in the defence against the aggression. That was -- those were the primary objectives, to organise life and defence in the territory inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And just after that, I then asked you, Did you support those objectives? And if I recall correctly, that you confirmed that you supported those objectives.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did support such objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were recruited as a member of the Intelligence Service by Brigadier Keza, it was probably relevant that you supported those goals of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, because if you hadn't supported those goals, you wouldn't have been an ideal person to work with military intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody who was involved in the defence against the aggressor supported the goals of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but here perhaps it is important to stress that as far as I know, Brigadier Keza was never a member of the Croatian Democratic Union community, and I don't think that that was important for him. For Brigadier Keza, what was important was that he received the right information at the right time, and he considered that I could provide him with that kind of information for the area, that I could be the man to do that. Now, the work of Brigadier Keza was evaluated through his reports, so it was vital for him to have the right information at the right time. And at that point in time, he thought that I was the man to provide this, I was the man for the job, and that's why he put me forward. And through the corresponding procedure, I was appointed to that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Brigadier Keza, is it correct that he was actually a member of the Croatian Army or he had come from the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he came from the Croatian Army. Brigadier Keza was born -- well, he was in the Territorial Defence Staff in Ljubuski because he's from Ljubuski. Now, whether he was a volunteer in the Croatian Army and arrived later as a volunteer, I really don't know. All I do know is that he was born in Ljubuski and that he's from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll see a bit later whether he was or was not. Let's first look at your position within the Main Staff, and for this I'd first like to refer you to a document. It's two documents earlier to the position where you are now. It's document 2D01352. 2D10352 [sic]. And, sir, what this is, this is a list of payments for December -- actually, I'd like to refer you to the very last page of the document. It's the last page in both the English as well as the B/C/S version. Actually, the second-last page in the English version, and it's the document dated 17 December 1992. It's from the HVO HZ-HB Main Staff, and it says it's the HVO December 1992 payroll. Do you have that document? It's the last page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, first off, this is signed by General Petkovic? That's his signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it is his signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So it's correct that he was authorising payment of salaries? He was involved in matters like that as chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Number 11 on the list, it says "Radmilo Jasak, reconnaissance units adviser." That's you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And it says your salary was 32.000. Would that have been dinar, or what currency would that have been?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The point is if we look earlier in the document -- well, first off, on the same document, number 1 is receiving 42.000. But if we look earlier in the document, we see that 32.000 is the lowest amount that is paid to anybody for this month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kruger. If you look at page 3, you'll find Zdravko Kordic, who only gets 22.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And while we're at it, on page 4 there is quite a number that only get 30.000, which is not much less, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the point that I want to make is that: If we just look at the amounts of salary being paid in a month to you, in comparison to what was being paid to other people, you were actually not a very senior person in this organisation, according to the payroll; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to Mr. Kruger, but might I be of assistance? If you look at individual documents, you'll see that these figures do not refer to the salaries in the same month. You have salaries for February 1993, for example, and for November 1992. And if I remember, the inflation was quite high, so it's questionable whether you can evaluate figures according to the different months to be able to establish whose salary was higher and lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of moving on, I'll pursue the point, but let's look at a different document and let's step off this document. Sir, let's look at the fourth document in your binder, and that's P01683, P01683. This is a document dated the 18th of March, 1993, and it's a stamp list of members of the Main Staff of the HVO of the HZ-HB for accreditation, and it's signed by Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you just confirm, is that Mr. -- no, it's not signed by Mr. Petkovic. That looks like a different signature. Do you know whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Zeljko Akrap's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was his position in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant chief of the Main Staff for education, training, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, we'll see in this document that number 7 is the name of Zarko Keza, do you see that, chief of Military Intelligence Service?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, my question is: The first six names that appear above that, the first one is Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, then Miro Andric, Blaz Andric, and then it goes down to Adem Zulovic, whom you've just referred to. Those first six names, are they the people in Mr. Petkovic's immediate circle as commander of the Main Staff, or chief of the Main Staff, rather, at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all people who were in the Main Staff at that time, but we can see here that Miro Andric's brother is there, and, yes, I can see that the adjutant -- anyway, they were all people working in the Main Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. But from number 7 to number 13 or maybe 14, would those be the members of the VOS at that stage, the Intelligence Service? Zarko Keza, Nikola Mikulic, Zeljko Kajic, you, Radmilo Jasak, Dinko Zebic, Ljubo Peric, and Zeljko Mikulic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Zeljko Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, and so it goes to number 14. Sir, these names, are they mentioned here in order of seniority?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's one chief, and he issued assignments to all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you're referring to Mr. Zarko Keza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes, Zarko Keza was the chief, and he issued orders and assignments to everybody else and organised the work of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Everybody else on this list, were they then at the same level of seniority? This is referring to the list number 8 to 14, the people working at the VOS.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along with Mr. Mikulic, Nikola Mikulic, he was deputy when Zarko Keza wasn't there. All the rest, all us others, were on the same level, on a par.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, this may be a time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, before the break we were still looking at your position within the Intelligence Service Section in the Main Staff, and I still want you to look at one or two further things in this regard. We have now established that your superior was Brigadier Keza. The person who acted as his deputy was Mr. Mikulic or Mr. Nikola Mikulic. Now, I have a document which I'm not going to show to you. I'll simply tell you what the document says. It says that Mr. Mikulic had the rank of colonel, or actually it says: "Establishment rank, major colonel." Is this correct? Was he a major or a colonel?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when this document was issued, he was neither a colonel or a major, as far as I know. He did not have a rank at the time. There were no ranks at all at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you see him as your superior?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered him a colleague. And when Mr. Keza wasn't there, he signed documents. And if neither of the two were there, then I personally signed the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Would you sign the document in the third place or could any of the other people who were at the same level as you within the Intelligence Section also sign if Mr. Keza or Mr. Mikulic were not present?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases when other people signed their own documents. However, in principle, it was either Mr. Keza or Mr. Mikulic who were there and signed the documents. If the matter was urgent, then the document was signed by whoever drafted it and reported to the chief about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you're referring to the chief now, are you referring to the chief of the Main Staff or your chief, Mr. Keza?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we're talking about the VOS department, and we're talking about the chief of that department, of the VOS department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, have a look at document P0805, P0805. This document is already in evidence. This is a document dated the 9th of July, 1996. My apologies, Your Honour, I've misspoken. It's P0805. Your Honour, I've got it wrong again. P08705. My apologies. I suppose that's what's called a senior moment. 8705. You have the document, sir? This document is dated in Mostar, the 9th of July, 1996, and it's signed by Lieutenant General Zivko Budimir. And the document says: "We submit in the attachment the list of HV officers that were employees of HVO Main Staff. Some of them are still in the HVO, but not in the HVO Main Staff." And if we look at the list, it starts off with "Mr. Slobodan Praljak," "Milivoj Petkovic," and it goes on, and number 14 is "Radmilo Jasak." Now, sir, my first question to you is: Were you a member of the Main Staff -- a member of the HV before you joined the Main Staff in 1992, or could you help us understand this document, please?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen this document before. I see that it was issued in 1996. I joined the Ministry of Defence on the 5th of August, 1994, so for two years I had already been in Zagreb when this document was issued. And when I was in the Main Staff, I was a member of the HVO. When I was with the Main Staff and I was the commander of the 4th Battalion, I was exclusively in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. So, sir, if this document is meant to say that in 1992 and 1993, you were a member of the HV while you were a member of the Main Staff, that's not correct in regard to you? It's an error, in other words?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992 and 1993, at that time I was a member of the Main Staff -- or, rather, the HVO and exclusively of the HVO. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, but while you were a member of the Main Staff in 1992 and 1993, you were aware that there were other members of the Main Staff who were, indeed, also -- or who had come from the Croatian Army or the HV, people such as General Praljak and General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that people arrived as volunteers and joined the HVO. They came as volunteers. They had defended Croatia, and then they volunteered to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina as members of the HVO. When they were in the HVO, they were commanders or chiefs of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's turn back to exactly what you were doing in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, so it's an either/or situation. Either the document we have before us contains an error, in other words, you have been included in the list as an officer of the Croatian Army, when, in fact, you only became such a member in 1994, then there is a mistake, and it is surprising to see that the Croatian Army can make a mistake, but anything can happen in life, or you're not telling the truth. In that case, you are playing with fire, because the Croatian Army, when it established this list, was able to check things out in detail. There's something I've noticed. The person who signed this document, Zivko Budimir, is also on the list at number 52. He is an officer of the Croatian Army, and he held a position. So he's signing a document which I'm sure he's very familiar with. There are some well-known names on this list, Praljak, Petkovic, Akrap, Percy [as interpreted], Tole, Skender, Kapular, and so on and so forth. So it's a mistake, is it? How could such a mistake have been made by these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document was issued by the Ministry of Defence or, rather, by the Main Staff of the HVO. And at the top it says: "A list of the members of the Croatian Army who were engaged in the Main Staff of the HVO," which means that at the time when this document was drafted in 1996, I was a member of the Croatian Army. And at the time when I was a member of the Main Staff of the HVO, I was not a member of the Croatian Army. And just to illustrate the point, let me tell you that at that time I did not even have Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, all the people who have the document in B/C/S will have noticed that there's something strange about the document. On page 1, the document stops at number 33. On page 2, it picks up at number 20, and then it follows the order until number 33. Seemingly, page 2 should be a follow-up to another page which we don't have, and page 1 should have the follow-up to it, but it doesn't. So there's something which is very difficult to understand when we look at the B/C/S version. But that's just a detail. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's turn to what you were precisely doing within the Main Staff as -- or in the Intelligence office. Now, you were based or you had your office in the Main Staff headquarters; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In an office adjoining that of Brigadier Keza?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In your office, did you receive -- or how did you obtain the intelligence that you were analysing or dealing with? Did you go into the field and collect it yourself? Let's ask that. Did you collect the evidence in the field yourself first?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received reports from operation zones, and sometimes we did tour the ground to inspect the units and talk to the people. Sometimes Mr. Keza would come to me, to my battalion, and sometimes we would go and made field inspections and draw attention to some things that should not be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript. The page on the screen, line 4, the witness said that they received reports from operation zones and from the CED, which stands for the Centre for Electronic Activity. And that latter source has been omitted from the interpretation, and I believe it should not have been because it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, could you just confirm that you also received information from the Centre for Electronic Activity or CED?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And those are the intercepts that you received?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was information received in the area from the surveillance of radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, did you, yourself, sit with the headphones, monitoring the radio channels, or did you receive that information from somebody else who was doing that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information from others who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, basically, you would receive information from others, for the most part, either electronic or in the form of reports, and then you would put together a report for your immediate superior, Brigadier Keza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several of us who did that, and through conversations and by observing what had been practiced before, and what we received at that moment, we prepared our reports, segregated by operation zones. And then that was all aggregated into one report which Brigadier Keza signed, and that report was sent to various addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And your contribution to the report would only be regarding the sector for which you had responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That primarily referred to that sector. However, if I had information about another sector, then we exchanged that information with the colleagues once when we saw each other's reports to check whether the information contained in the report is the initial information or the repetition of something that had happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And from Brigadier Keza, who consolidated these contributions from your level, the report went up to General Petkovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And from Brigadier Petkovic, would that report or could that report then also go further up to, for instance, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such reports, as a rule, were sent to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic once they were completed at our end. They were sent at the same time. We did not have to send it to the chief of the Main Staff and Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In the intelligence that you received, I take it that you also received intelligence regarding alleged crimes committed by members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean when you say "crimes." We received information about the enemy. We received that information from our staff on the ground. The task of the Intelligence Service was to observe the activities of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you obtain any information, within that function, that the HVO was committing crimes against the enemy at any stage? Didn't you hear about anything?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any information about crimes committed by the HVO. We did not monitor that. We observed the activities of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You personally -- in your time in the Intelligence Service, did you ever personally -- apart from intelligence that you received, did you become aware of any alleged crimes being committed by members of the HVO in any area?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not learn about crimes committed by the HVO in any of the areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look further at exactly what you were doing or how you were doing this and explore this. Your evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a follow-up question for you. As you know, we are getting closer to the end of this trial. After a number of years, we have a whole swathe of documents and we are beginning to have a better idea. We have a video that shows the capture of ABiH soldiers on the 9th of May. We see the ABiH soldiers who are lined up next to each other, and they are being captured. That is the "enemy," quote/unquote, who is being captured. These soldiers, unfortunately for their sake, are going to disappear, and their bodies will be found later with identification marks; a watch, for instance. My first question: At the time in May, in your position, had you seen this report showing the capture of ABiH soldiers at the headquarters of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I saw that report on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you saw that on TV. Now, what I would like to know is: As an analyst, at a later stage did you ask yourself what happened to those soldiers, or did you just move on and you did not really deal with the whereabouts of those soldiers who were part of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't give it much thought. I assumed that they had been captured somewhere and that they were somewhere -- in prison somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to follow up on a question that was asked by Mr. Kruger, but he did not go into details, and I don't know really why. From what I understood, you were an analyst, and then the report is sent to your superior, Zaka [as interpreted], and then the report is sent to and -- the chief of staff, to the commander of the HVO, and then you are not quite sure where this report goes. You do not know whether it is sent to Mr. Stojic, who is the minister of defence or the head of the Defence Department. You don't know. All you do know is that it's sent to your superior, and then you assume that this report is sent to the head of the Main Staff of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all our reports, intelligence reports, were sent directly to the chief of the Main Staff and the head of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I was wondering whether, at your level, you were aware of what was at stake with your work, because we have seen quite a few documents. I could show them to you, but we are not going to look into details. The head of the Main Staff would use some intelligence and to say to the international community or to Pasalic, This is what is happening right now. So what you were doing was actually very important. Were you aware of what was at stake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we were conscious of the fact that we were doing an important job and that it was of service to the chief and to others so that they could make their decisions, and we did our job to the best of our abilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Still on this topic, now, you said during your evidence-in-chief you testified on the 19th of January last week, and it's at transcript reference T-48584, at line 5. The question was: "Would your chief normally inform you of any information received elsewhere, at other meetings or in a different way, pertaining to anything that the service was in charge of?" And your response at line 8 was: "He informed us regularly about everything he believed was required for our work." Now, sir, this is correct; you stand by what you said here, isn't it? It's correct, Brigadier Keza informed you about everything he believed was required for your work?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So is it correct that you were on a "need to know" basis and your boss, Brigadier Keza, didn't necessarily tell you everything that he knew?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that. I can't know whether Brigadier Keza knew something more than he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Exactly. And also Brigadier --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, when we were compiling a report dealing with a certain area, and if he knew the kind of work we were doing, if he had some information on his part about that, then he would convey it to us so that we could incorporate it into our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, you also said Brigadier Keza, he co-operated with SIS at his level, but you didn't co-operate with SIS at your level; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I did not know who the people were in SIS, what positions they occupied, and what their remit was. We didn't have anything to do with that. The chiefs of the services at a higher level would exchange information amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And all you would receive or know about those meetings would be whatever Brigadier Keza chose to pass on to you if he believed it was required for your work; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew what Brigadier Keza told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And so you weren't in the management component of the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'll elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: With management of the Main Staff, I would think that the most senior officers, heads of section in the Main Staff, would probably meet with the chief of the Main Staff, General Petkovic, and that they would hold meetings to decide on strategy and direction and activities, and these would mean meetings which would then filter down to the other members of the Main Staff, the workers. My question is: You weren't a member of that top echelon which met regularly with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may object at this point, Your Honour. And I hesitate to object, but if you look at the question, it said that "they would probably meet with." It appears that the question calls for speculation. Now, if the gentleman doesn't know -- if my learned friend doesn't know, he might want to ask an open-ended question to get the information as a predicate, but it seems to me that he's asking the gentleman to guess. This is the first time I hear of the word "management" in the military context. Now, so he's asking the witness to guess. If he knows for sure, he's to say that they were meeting, and give us an example and what have you. Otherwise, I would suggest that he rephrase the question or ask the gentleman an open-ended question how things were done, and then he could go on and explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, without speculating, please listen carefully. Earlier on, the Prosecutor asked you whether you had been aware of crimes that had been committed by the HVO, and your answer was, No. Very well. Then the Prosecutor moves on to something else, and he's asking you whether there were some contacts between the SIS and your chief, Zerka [as interpreted], and you're saying, Yes. The third line of questioning, because everything makes sense, the Prosecutor is putting to you that sometimes your chief would give you some information, but you did not know whether the items of information that were given to you were complete or not. And I understood your answer perfectly. So I'm going to give you a very clear example. We received some evidence stating that the SIS in Prozor issued a lot of reports on acts committed by police officers from the HVO; theft, violence, and so on and so forth. I'm not going to go into details. This is an SIS document, and I assume that this document from the Prozor SIS was sent the hierarchal way to higher levels, and the chief at the same level as yours, so within the SIS, may have said to your chief, We have learnt that in Prozor, some police officers are behaving in such a way that would be a cause of concern, and your chief could have said something to you or maybe said nothing to you. So, you see, everything really holds together without really speculating at all. So what I would like to know is whether at some stage your chief said, I learned from the SIS that in Prozor there were some problems. So, you see, this is a very clear example and a very clear question that I'm putting to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the chief didn't convey that information to me, perhaps because it was outside the remit of my work, my primary work. Perhaps it went beyond that scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, or perhaps the chief working at the SIS did not tell him of anything. That could be possible as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kruger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, return to the previous point. Your chief, did he meet with General Petkovic at times when you were not present?
