utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the Main Staff and the chief of VOS could meet whenever they felt the inclination to do so because there was just a door between the two offices. They didn't have to go into the hallway at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But my question is: You didn't attend each and every meeting between them, you weren't privy to every discussion they had, General Petkovic and Brigadier Keza?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you attend meetings that Brigadier -- General Petkovic held with other heads of sections in the Main Staff on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that at the level of the Main Staff they had regular meetings or that there were any premises where the meetings took place. I don't have any information about that happening in the Main Staff, so I can't know when General Petkovic might have called some of the heads of the other departments to a meeting. I know that I would talk to General Petkovic myself quite a few times at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: On the 19th of January, and this is transcript reference 48579, line 11, you said: "I learned this from the chief of the Military Intelligence Service, who told me that he had been informed about this by General Petkovic." So the whole point that I'm making, sir, is that you weren't at such a level that you were the confidant of General Petkovic in the Main Staff during your time there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question. What do you mean "confidant," the confidant of? As I say, I talked to General Petkovic a number of times, and I think the talks were sincere, frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: General Petkovic didn't tell you each and every single bit of information that he was privy to; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really do think I have to object to that kind of question because it is truly asking the witness to speculate. How can the witness know whether General Petkovic told him every single bit of information and so on? I think this type of question is quite out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, please be cautious, because there will be objections and we're going to waste time. And I draw the conclusion that the trial is not resting on this and that everyone is wasting one's time, so please be very clear, very precise, ask him whether he was meeting General Petkovic. And, if so, what were they talking about; were they talking about the weather or about work? And he's going to say we were talking about work, and then you proceed. I would not have this problem, because I know in advance how to avoid those sorts of issues and objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, my point to you is that: At your level, you only had a partial picture of what was going on with regard to the HVO actions in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Main Staff, at the highest level. There is no higher level than the Main Staff. In the Military Intelligence Service, I took part in the drafting of reports. We would receive information from the ground, what was going on behind enemy lines, and we would send out these reports to the highest level, the chief of the Main Staff and the head of the Defence Department. There was no higher level than that, so I don't know in what context to understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't have access to each and every bit of intelligence because that's how intelligence services work. Intelligence is kept compartmentalised, isn't that so, to protect it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have access to information from all the operations zones because my colleagues created these reports and information, and I mostly dealt with the Mostar area, which means that I was informed of the reports, once they were completed, and everything that came in, all the documents that came in to be processed for South-East Herzegovina. They all arrived, and all we had was -- to do was to reduce it and summarise it into these reports. So information linked to the enemy did come in and were collected in one place. It was all in one room. We were all in one room, sitting 'round a round table, if you will, except for the head of VOS, Keza, who had his own office. Otherwise, all the rest of us were in the same office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, but by your own admission, you don't know what information was available from SIS, so you simply did not have a complete picture of things, of events. You were working only on the intelligence that you were lucky enough to be made aware of. You didn't have a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but I have to object again. What does that mean, a complete picture? Nobody had a complete picture anywhere on this earth, nor will the Judges have a complete picture of everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, your objection is irrelevant and the question is what it is, and the witness is about to answer and you are taking the floor. I think that you are doing this for nothing. This is very simple. The person is -- well, please wait. This person is working in military intelligence. The Prosecutor wants to know whether military intelligence was coupled with intelligence coming from the SIS, in order for the chief of the Main Staff to be aware of everything that was going on. This is the case for the Prosecution. And he says that he knew about everything that was going on on the military side, so why do you want to take the floor here? What are you doing here, except wasting time?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has already answered the question about information from SIS, and this is the sixth question we're hearing on the same topic and you're allowing it. Now, what I want to react to is the following sentence: "You were working only on the intelligence that you were lucky enough to be made aware of." And I think that that is quite improper because the question contains several sentences. And if we want a yes-or-no answer from this witness, what part of the sentence will he be answering? Now, if you think that questions of this kind are proper, then I apologise for intervening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you wanted to answer. Please answer, because you were interrupted by counsel. You were about to say something. What were you about to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was getting ready to say that the information that was coming in from SIS sometimes, SIS did not deal with the enemy. Very few pieces of information were coming in, and we would get it from our chief. But what should have been the primary matter was that we received them from the CED and the operations zone, and we based our reports on that. They were what they were, in conformity with our abilities and the information that we were able to come by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, if I understand correctly, you said that information coming from the SIS did not have necessarily to do with the enemy, because as far as the enemy was concerned, you were the one in charge of gathering information and intelligence, so you had the first line of intelligence for the ABiH and not the SIS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, because the SIS could arrive at some information quite by chance, and then that information would be conveyed further. But the prime task of VOS was to deal with the enemy, not SIS's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you're not in a position to tell this Chamber whom General Petkovic consulted in his decision-making processes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as General Petkovic is concerned, when it came to the enemy, then it was exclusively the VOS, whereas for all the rest, he had other people to deal with other affairs. That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And all those other people who advised him, you weren't privy to their -- to what they were advising specifically to General Petkovic, were you; not in all instances, at least?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody can know everything. Everybody knows which piece of the pie he's in charge of, and you need to gain a complete picture with all the information put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Exactly, sir, and that's the whole point, that you only knew your little bit of the pie. And all your testimony that you've been giving so far is based on only that little piece of the pie that you were aware of; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've said so far I said as a worker of VOS and as a worker of the Main Staff, because I served in the Main Staff, to which all the information came, so I was -- I could have been informed about those matters too. So I'm speaking also as an inhabitant of the town of Mostar, where I lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, but still the question remains, and that the testimony that you gave last week, the opinions that you expressed on various matters, is based principally on that little bit of the pie that you had knowledge about. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object to the tendentious phrase "little bit of the pie." How big the bit of the pie is, isn't that a matter for Your Honours' judgement, based on his evidence? Of course, Mr. Kruger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think you're quite right, absolutely right. I was already suggesting that you cut out the word "small."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Beyond that, there is a question as to whether it's just not blindingly obvious to keep saying to a witness, You could only tell us what you knew on the basis of what you knew. But if Mr. Kruger wants to spend time on that, it's his decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, you know that Judges are ruling the way the questionings are being run. I believe that you have a case, namely, that this witness is not aware of everything. And the witness states that military intelligence was dealt with by himself, by his colleagues, by his chief, and by Petkovic, and so he doesn't agree with your case. If you have any evidence to the contrary, you have to show this evidence. Otherwise, it's going to last for a long time. You're going to say, Yes, and he's going to say, No, or vice versa, so he's going to say, They were in charge of military intelligence, and only them; there was nobody else in charge of military intelligence. So if you have any other evidence that would go against what he's saying, then it's for you to provide those. Otherwise, it could last for hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll finish with this. I have only one question regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, are you willing to at least agree with me that if I were to show you other evidence which you were not privy to, that would change some of the views that you expressed last week? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that as well. He can't -- Mr. Kruger can't possibly make that suggestion until and unless he does put such evidence. He can't ask the witness to say, in advance, What you show me, I don't know what it is, will change my mind. That's up to Mr. Kruger to demonstrate it, if he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the Military Intelligence Service, VOS, is it correct that it did not only pass information on to General Petkovic and Mr. Stojic, but it also made recommendations at times?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, there were some recommendations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at Exhibit P02760, 2760.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, in which binder is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's still binder 1, still the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document is a document from 14 June 1993. It's an information proposal, and it's from the head of the HVO Main Staff, VOS, Zarko Keza. And if we could just confirm, is that Brigadier Keza's signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Brigadier Keza's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on 14 June, he says, and this is the first paragraph: "A number of sources have informed us that the Muslim army is launching all-out attacks on the territories of Central Bosnia and Northern Herzegovina, committing crimes, and more serious -- much more serious than those committed by the Serbs." My first question is: You were informed about crimes committed by the ABiH or the Muslims and by the Serbs, but you didn't receive information about crimes -- any crimes committed by the HVO members? I just need to get that straight.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not learn of any HVO crimes. I did not have an occasion to see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at what you propose or what is being proposed by the VOS. And number 1 says that: "The term 'BH Army' be replaced in official usage with 'the Muslim forces.'" Now, were you aware of such a proposal being made?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you perhaps tell the Chamber what was behind this proposal?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. What was behind this proposal was the wish to demonstrate clearly, when it comes to reporting, that journalists should not try and create a wrong image in the general public about the BiH Army as being composed of multiple ethnicities and that it defended Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, it was exclusively composed of Muslims, and at that time it attacked the areas under the control of the HVO. An impression was being created that when one said the BiH Army, that that implied the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the impression that was created by the media for the general public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, number 2 says: "The real and complete mobilisation of human and material resources be conducted in the HZ-HB or Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Now, sir, from your previous answer, can I take it that this complete mobilisation of resources, human resources, would also relate to the mobilisation of Muslims within the HZ-HB or would this relate only to Croats?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This referred to human resources. However, when it came to the territories where conflicts were underway already, those units were mobilised of all the men that were available in Mostar and Konjic, and this refers more to the areas where there were no war activities going on, such as municipalities which were not affected by the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But, sir, from the second bullet, do you mean that this, indeed, means that potentially Muslim members of the HVO can also be mobilised against the Muslim forces? Is this what's contemplated?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely that was not the case. This refers to the areas of Grude, Siroki Brijeg, and other municipalities that did not have any Muslim population at all; Posusje and some others of the kind which were not directly affected by the war. That's why people there could not be engaged to help with the defence of the areas that were affected by the war. Those areas that were affected by the war, there was nobody to mobilise. Those who had not fled were already involved and were already members of the units that were fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 says: "Muslim men of military age be forbidden to enter or leave the Republic of Croatia." So what about a Muslim member of the HVO who wants to return from Croatia to his unit? So according to this order, he would be forbidden -- or this proposal, he would be forbidden from returning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bullet point 3 was drafted, and maybe here it's not really clear as to what it should have meant. What I'm saying is we did have information that Muslim fighters or military conscripts, members of the ABiH, who are leaving to spend some time with their families on the Croatian coast. Their families were there, accommodated by the Croatian government and fed by the Croatian authorities. After having spent some time resting there with their wives and children, they returned to the territories of Central Bosnia and North Herzegovina and again engaged in fighting against the HVO. So that is the context within which this bullet point 3 was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, paragraph 4, that says: "All Croatian men of military age in the Republic of Croatia who fled the Republic of BH for whatever reason be detained and handed over to the HVO ..." Weren't you, in the VOS, concerned at all with Muslim members of the HVO or Muslim members liable for service in the HVO who had fled to Croatia; didn't you want those people back as well?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question properly. Maybe I can comment on what is written in here. This was written in a time rife with panic. There was a threat that Croatians would completely disappear from the territories of Central Bosnia and Western or Northern Herzegovina. The situation was dire, and the tone is panicky, because all attempts were made to get hold of soldiers by hook or by crook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we'll come back to these matters a bit later. Let's look at just paragraph 6, finally: "Two elite HV/Croatian Army/or HVO brigades be sent along the main axes, the main axis being Prozor-Scipe village-Parsovici-Fojnica, with the aim to lift the blockade ..." So you were aware in the VOS that HV units, Croatian Army units, could be commandeered or utilised?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely not aware of that. This was a panicky reaction. Assistance is sought from anybody who might have been able to help. We did not have any information about this, and this is not all within the remit of the VOS. This is not an ordinary situation. The grounds were being lost. The agreements that were signed at the top were not being observed. The hostilities were not stopped, and there was a threat that the Croatian populous would completely disappear from the territories of Central Bosnia and Northern Herzegovina. Then you do whatever if you think that you will be able to get assistance and help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So you're saying that your superior, Brigadier Keza, was prepared to put this in his report, recommending or proposing that Croatian Army units be used, without knowing whether that was possible at all? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that he didn't know what could be done, because you see here the HVO or the HV, anybody who can help, there was no information as to what was possible. The appeal is launched to whoever was in a position to help prevent the complete disappearance of Croats from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I have to press you on this. I'm not convinced. This is a proposal by the head of the VOS to the chief of the Main Staff, Brigadier -- General Petkovic, and it says: "We propose that you utilise two elite Croatian Army units." On what basis would he make that recommendation if he didn't know it was possible?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say here "two elite units of the Croatian Army." It says "two elite units of the Croatian Army or the HVO," or anybody else, which means that you are looking for anybody, anybody who could help save those people. There was a huge number of refugees. Villages had been burned down, according to our information. There was at the time, according to our estimate, a very clear possibility that the HVO would be militarily defeated completely in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's step off this document. Now, before going to binder number 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Kruger, you are stepping off this document. I have questions to put to you. This document shows that your service was -- or department was aware of a great number of things, and what is very surprising in this document is to look at recipients 4 and 5. The document is being sent to Zagreb and to Split Operational Zone, Colonel Binazimo [phoen]. When I read this, I realised that the VOS fell within the remit of other entities. Mr. Boban -- had I been in had Mr. Boban's shoes, I would not have been happy about this. So, you know, negotiations were ongoing in Geneva. The question of the armed forces of the ABiH - and the HVO, a component of the ABiH, was being addressed, and this document, it is being asked to change - someone is asking to change the system. In logistical terms, if I had been in Mr. Stojic's shoes I wouldn't have been happy because logistical questions are being addressed. Had I been in the shoes of Mr. Tudjman, I be saying, Well, what is he doing, why is he such a busy-body? The Croats who have fled the Republic of Croatia, why do they have to be handed over? It's interfering in the sovereign affairs of Croatia, and so on and so forth. So what is he doing when he asks for troops -- elite troops of the Croatian Army to be sent in, when the international community was very careful in that regard? Zarko Keza intervenes or interferes in areas which he might not be entitled to. There could be three reasons for this: A, what you said, the situation is disastrous; B, he is in a strong position because nobody can go against him, and he therefore interferes in other areas; or, C, the third reason, on the fourth and fifth -- at paragraph 4 and 5, Zagreb and Split are being informed, and therefore the Croatian Army is entirely involved in all these events, and therefore he refers to the authorities mentioned in paragraph 4 and 5. And, therefore, your services, the VOS, plays a crucial role which goes well beyond mere military intelligence. You are coming up with political suggestions which have to do with questions of sovereignty. You were working for this service. Is this document a good illustration of what you were actually doing, or did your superior go beyond what he was entitled to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is one of the rare documents which was written in this way, and it really demonstrates the gravity of the situation and the seriousness of the situation. As far as bullet points 4 and 5 are concerned, they talk about the exchange of information that arrived from the territory, and the focus of that was from the previous period, talking about the information received about the Army of Republika Srpska and its movements in the hinterland of Dubrovnik and other areas where it was interesting. So this was an exchange of information. It was not sent to the chief of staff or others. It was sent to the Military Intelligence Service, to the addressees referred to herein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just finally on this document, to just get it on the record as well, that this proposal was sent to Mr. Boban and Mr. Stojic, in addition to General Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's move to the last document I'm going to show you in this binder. Two documents further on in the binder is document P03622, 3622. Now, I saw from the summary of your evidence, and listening to your testimony, that you made the point that there were many more officers in the operational zones than within the Main Staff. Is that correct, you did make that point?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already spoken about the percentage of men, and I said that the percentage was higher when it came to the officer staff. And that percentage was higher at lower levels, and those people were familiar with the areas. Their activities were exclusively defensive. They defended the territory of their respective municipalities, and that's why we had a problem with mobilisations. We talked about that just a minute ago. Municipalities which were not directly affected by combat activities were reluctant to send their inhabitants to the territories of other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document is a document by -- or an order, rather, by General Petkovic. It's dated the 21st of July, 1993. And this is a period when you were still in the VOS at the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this period, I was in Sector South [as interpreted], but I was on the VOS list and I was acting as an assistant to Miro Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to correct the transcript. The witness didn't say "Sector South," he said "Sector North," Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, could you just confirm that you did, indeed, refer to Sector North? You were attached to Sector North; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sector North. I said "Sector North, with Miro Andric."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we look at this order, and just above the order it says: "To establish the true situation and take concrete measures, I hereby order:" And then number 1: "A Main Staff HVO team (enclosure 1) of 21 July 1993 shall visit all sectors held by our units." Then number 2: "The team shall ascertain the situation in the zones of responsibility, the number of men in units, the number of men on the lines, the level of integration of the defence system, the enforcement of the sectors, the command structure, morale of soldiers, the ability of units to perform tasks, supply levels of all types of ammunition, and deployment of anti-aircraft defence equipment." Paragraph 3 says: "The control team shall issue orders on the spot aimed at rectifying established shortcomings." Now, sir, my question to you. General Petkovic is ordering this, and he's sending a team from the Main Staff to check certain things within the operational zones, and then he's also authorising this team to set certain problems right if they identify them in the areas they're investigating. Is this a fair assessment, as you understand the document?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fair assessment. The control teams will issue an order to correct any possible mistakes or shortcomings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the mistakes would include rectifying, for instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. This -- Mr. Kruger referred -- it's in line 9 in my transcript, anyway, to -- within the operational zones. We observe this document is only dealing with a single operational zone. That's quite clear from the document, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies, I did misspeak. This, indeed, refers to only one single operational zone. But the question remains. "The team is sent to rectify matters in that operational zone, which could include the command structure."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this appears to me, would you agree, to indicate that General Petkovic is, indeed, the superior of all officers within that operational zone?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see here that General Petkovic was the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. He established a control team. There is no attachment that would enable me to tell you who was in charge of what. And in bullet point 4, it says: "Daily reports to be submitted to the chief of the General Staff by 2200 hours." This means that he had established a team that would ascertain what the situation was on the ground, because he was not sure that he had been receiving proper information from the ground. And in the heading, you can see that this was received by the OZ South-East Herzegovina. You can see that from the incoming stamp. You can see that this was done to control the defence zone. This order concerned the defence zone and was meant to check whether men were positioned well for defence in order to prevent the implementation of the plan to connect the territory with the sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question of qualification, because here, of course, as we heard, Mr. Stewart has raised the issue that it was only relating to a single operational zone. I would like to ask the witness what is his view on the question of a difference between sectors and zones of responsibility. On page 1, the English text of this particular Defence Department order, you will see that on the left hand, under "The HVO Main Staff," et cetera, et cetera, you will find "control of the sectors," and below that one it is written "zones of responsibilities," "zones," in plural, "of responsibility." It is, of course, also true that on the right hand the addressee is always at "JIH South-East Herzegovina Operations Zone." So my question is: If apart from these zones of responsibility, what particular issue was covered by the sectors, that is, the control of the sectors? It is my question to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this order here was written, and where you see where it says "the control of the sector-defence zone," to explain this I would like to say that this was the area of defence that was controlled by one sector. At the time, the defence zone of South-East Herzegovina was under constant attacks by the BH Army after the 30th of June, and that's why the zone was divided into three sectors. There's Sector North, the city of Mostar, and Sector South. This means that the operational zone was divided into three separate sectors, and this order here was written in order to take stock of the real situation in the three zones. There were all constant demands dealing with the lack of soldiers, lack of ammunition, lack of armament, and that's why a team had to be established to see what the situation truly was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to thank Judge Prandler for having drawn our attention to the translation of this document. If we look at the Croatian document, we will see that it speaks about the defence zone, and that's singular "the defence zone," whereas in the English text this has been translated as "the zones of responsibility," in plural, and the word "defence" has been replaced by the word "responsibility." Therefore, we are talking about a mistranslation. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Kruger. I was aware of that. Still on this document, if I understand this document correctly, Mr. Petkovic receives reports, and they are cause of concern because they are contradictory information, and he decides, given that he's the one drafting the document, as you can see that there are initials "MP," so I assume that he is the one drafting those documents, and he can request for a mission to be sent to shed some light. I see that next to the initials of "MP," you have initials "DS," and when you look at a document of the members of the Main Staff in 1992, there is a "Darko Sutalo," "DS." So I'm wondering whether we're talking about the same person here or whether we're talking about somebody else. But if we are dealing with Darko Sutalo, we have a slight problem because Darko Sutalo was an analyst at the time. So according to you, who is "DS" working at the Main Staff in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't remember, but I don't think that Darko Sutalo was there at the time. If this referred to "Sutalo," then "S" would have a diacritic. Here we see "MP/DS" and "DS" is the typist, whereas "MP" is the general wrote this document in his own hand and gave it to the typist to type. So it's really not important who the second person is represented by the second set of initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're not going to waste any more time. Please proceed, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to try and finish with this document before the break. I have only about two questions or three questions. Sir, the fact that in this order General Petkovic authorises his -- the people he appoints in this -- in this team to, for instance, change the command structure or rectify the command structure, do you agree that this means that the Main Staff has the authority to go into an operational zone and exert its authority on the place?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a very critical period, riddled with a lot of problems in the OZ South-East Herzegovina. Three sectors were created from one OZ, and here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but the question is not what the situation was. The question is simply: General Petkovic, in the Main Staff, had that authority to go into an operational zone and take decisions and impose their decisions at that place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were defence zones. General Petkovic could issue an order, either written or oral, to the command of the OZ, but this is an order to rectify mistakes. For example, if you see that the position is not in a good place, that in one place you have one soldier, whereas you have four soldiers in another place, and you're expecting an attack, then you can distribute their numbers evenly, and you put two in one place and three in the other place. The most important thing is that at 2200 hours every day, reports ought to have been sent as to what had been done in the field. If something was still not good and not properly done, then General Petkovic still could intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, from this, and this will be the last point I raise before the break, I put it to you that up until July 1993, General Petkovic was the top soldier in the military pyramid of the HVO. He was at the top, and every other soldier or officer who was beneath him in that pyramid was subordinate to his command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that General Petkovic was the chief of the Main Staff and that there was a military pyramid. Every member of the HVO was under the Main Staff but also had his own commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the operational zones and their commanders also formed part of the pyramid underneath General Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, the translation hasn't been recorded. Could you just repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, OZs were also under the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And just a final question. When General Praljak became commander of the Main Staff, he became the top soldier on the pinnacle of that pyramid, and General Petkovic became number 2 beneath him; is that correct? This is July 1993.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, towards the end of July 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honour, this may be a time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, we're going to have a break of 20 minutes. We'll resume at around 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Colonel, since we are going to finish at 7.00, I don't want to forget to tell you that we will have our next hearing at 9.00 a.m. tomorrow morning. Mr. Kruger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, now we're stepping over to binder number 2 now. We finished with binder number 1, and I'd now like to talk to you about Konjic. Thank you, Mr. Usher. I'd now like to talk to you about Konjic, and for the next hour or so that's what we'll be dealing with. But just to orient ourselves that we know exactly what we're talking about and that we have a picture in our minds, could you turn to the map at P09276, 9276. Your Honour, I'm informed that the map number plus 1 is the e-court reference. It's page 10 in e-court, for the Registry, in looking for it. 9276. Sir, if you can look at it on the screen, that's just as good. Sir, this map is already in evidence, and it represents the ethnic composition of the municipalities in Bosnia in 1991, so this is according to the information obtained from the census in 1991. And what I'd like to focus you on is, first of all, the municipality of Konjic. Do you see the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, you see that on this map, the colour is grey, and the legend is that this is a municipality with an absolute Muslim majority, greater than 50 per cent. And you knew that, that's correct, isn't it, that Konjic had an absolute Muslim majority, the population?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you see Jablanica municipality, just to the left of Konjic, and that's the same; that was also a Muslim-majority municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And then above Prozor, you have Gornji Vakuf, and that's also a Muslim-majority municipality, and that's correct too?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In between Gornji Vakuf and Jablanica, that's Prozor, and Prozor had an absolute Croat majority. You agree with that as well?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you see the blue line that's drawn on this map, and is it correct that that would represent the boundary of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as it was established in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, is "boundary" the same as "border"? What exactly, because if I look at this, and we look -- is Brcko, the entire Brcko area is in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that what the gentleman is saying at this point in time and throughout? So what does he mean by "boundary"? I know it says "on a map." Does he mean "border"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you were aware of the establishment, you said, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And looking at this map, is it correct that Gornji Vakuf, Jablanica, and Konjic fell within the area that was being claimed as part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's drawn here is something that I see for the first time, these borders here or boundaries. But the area, as an area, Herceg-Bosna, as far as I know, I've never seen any borders of any kind. But in the area of Konjic and Gornji Vakuf, there were villages where you had a majority Croat population, so only those villages were considered to be within the organisation of Herceg-Bosna, with respect to the organisation of life and defence and so on. It was not considered that whole municipalities, to the best of my knowledge, were within it and that Herceg-Bosna had some fixed borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The good thing about this map is that it's in colour, and it represents the ethnic composition according to the census in 1991. And you pointed out that it was boundaries and not borders. These are the boundaries and not the borders. The only question that I have regarding this map -- I've already seen this map, but every time you look at a map again, you get more information. But I'm rather surprised by Kupres. Kupres seems to be a municipality with a Serb majority, and I'm wondering why it is included in the Croat Community. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I do. I'm not looking at this as administrative borders or anything like that, and I've never seen anything like this drawn, but Kupres did have some villages who were -- where the Croatians were in the majority. So this referred only to those villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you said that in the Kupres municipality, there were villages with a Croatian majority. You are probably right. I'm not going to doubt this, but I was wondering why the entire municipality is in red, the entirety of the municipality is in red. Does that mean that they are more than 50 per cent Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this -- yes, that's right, Your Honour. This is a map which was obviously drawn according to a 1991 population census, and the whole municipality is red because there was a Serb majority of over 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could you please explain why is it that a municipality with over 50 per cent of Serbs finds itself one fine day in an area or in boundaries -- I'm not talking about borders here; I'm not talking about a state here. But how could a municipality like that find itself in an area which is referred to as Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, within these borders I didn't see this as being a purely Croatian area. There were certain enclaves within these municipalities where we went to help people to organise their defence and life and work in those municipalities, so I've never seen any boundaries like that or borders drawn in this way. It's the Kupres municipality which was included only because it had some Croatian villages which organised themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let's look at another map which shows Konjic more closely, and this is P11191, P11191. It would be about the sixth document from the end, sir. Now, sir, this is a map of Konjic municipality, drawn up reflecting the 1991 census outcome. Have you ever seen maps like these before?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maps like this were drawn once the census in 1991 was completed and when we knew which villages, according to the census, had what population; which were Croatian, and Muslim, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And this -- if you look at the figures at the top, it shows clearly what you've already acknowledged, that Croats were about 11.500, while Muslims were about 23.800, and that's the absolute majority of Muslims. So you don't dispute those numbers?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dispute the numbers, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we look further at the map, you'll see that there are green dots and there are red dots, and then there are also blue dots. The green dots refer to centres where there are Muslim populations, and the red dots refer to centres where there are Croat populations. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the town of Konjic, we see that it has a big green circle surrounding "Konjic." Do you understand that to mean that the population of Konjic was a majority of Muslim people or Muslim inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think some care is needed here, because the legend makes it pretty clear what the difference is between solid circles and simply a circle where the circumference only is in colour. It's a distinction between absolute and relative majorities, so we probably ought to proceed with precision on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The point that I would like to make on this is: If we look at the town of Konjic, we see a few red dots in the vicinity, but specifically Zaslivlje, Zabrdje, and Turija. Do you see those three dots, red dots?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zaslivlje, Zabrdje, and Turija. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, these three towns or these three locations, did they eventually become an HVO enclave, or at one stage they became an HVO enclave in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did become that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So we'll be dealing with them at a later stage. Let's just find one further place. If we go east from the town of Konjic -- sorry, west from the town of Konjic to the border of Prozor -- Jablanica, sorry, and we go up about a centimetre, we find a little red dot saying "Radesine," do you see that, "Radesine?" Do you see that? It's just above "Ribici." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where Radesine is. It's the village of Radesine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the HVO, during the course of 1993, had established a check-point at that location?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Radesine, you had the HVO. Whether it was a check-point I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1993 was, well, an abnormally long year. Perhaps we would invite a bit more precision in what's being put to the witness as to when in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll get back to this. And the main point is just locating it on the map, so when we do get to it, that everybody at least has an idea of where these locations are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, according to your testimony on the meaning of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the way I understand your testimony would mean that if we look at the most northern red dot in the municipality of Konjic, that's a little village named "Pozetva." You see that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pozetva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, according to your testimony, where you say, No, no, we were only -- or the inclusion in the HZ-HB would only be of villages where Muslims stayed, if I understand you correctly, does that mean that Pozetva would be included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? My apology, I misspoke. I referred to villages where Muslims stayed. I meant villages where Croats stayed. So only villages where Croats stayed would be included or would fall in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that what you meant, or rather would Pozetva be included?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be included, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if we look at Buscak, which is about two centimetres or three centimetres north of Konjic, that would be included, just to follow through on the argument?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And so according to what you're saying, the HVO would establish its administration over such villages?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was to establish a defence for those Croats and everybody else who wanted to stand up to the enemy, because there was nothing before that. Not exclusively for the Croats, but for everybody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, let's move on from there, at least if we have an idea of what we're looking at. And just before I show you a videotape, I'd just like to check with you. Are you aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. Colonel, I listened to your answer. You said that the HVO wanted to establish a defence line. And a while ago Mr. Kruger asked you a question about the village of Radesine, about the fact that there was a check-point there, and you said that you didn't know about that. But I am concerned when I see this map and when I compare it with the previous maps. The Konjic municipality in the previous map, one -- it looks as if it should be under Croatian control. On looking at this map, however, in the presence of three different ethnic groups, the Serbs, the Croats and the Muslims, this is quite blinding. How could the ones control the others, in light of the lay of the land and the way these municipalities are intermingled and everything is extremely complicated? When you say that the HVO established defence lines, in your view, does this mean that the HVO wanted to remain in its position, without conquering anything further afield, or in order to solve the situation they needed to conquer those villages indicated in blue on the map or in green, simply because one was Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are very specific questions and situations, and it changed from one month to the next. So when we hear 1993 mentioned for the village of Radesine, for example - the Prosecutor mentioned that - I know -- well, I don't know what period he has in mind, but I know that in the village of Radesine, you had Croats who were included and who were part of the HVO, and at the time, if they did anything, they did it for defence purposes. Now, if we look at 1992, for example, then the Croats, together with the Muslims, were holding the lines facing the Army of Republika Srpska. So it depended on what period you had in mind and which year. So here the HVO wanted to protect the Croats, regardless of where they be. That was the primary goal, to organise them against the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serbian foe, the Serbian enemy, so all the people who wanted to join the HVO, the HVO assisted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you were saying that we need to look at this map one year after the other. This map is the result of the 1991 census, and we may well ask the question, Does this map apply to 1993? Looking at Trusina, if you look at the village of Trusina - much has been said about this village - it is a Croatian village on this map. From what I understood, in April 1993, a few days before Ahmici, this village was conquered by the ABiH and Croats are killed. In that case, the red dot that we see here where Trusina is located then becomes a green dot; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did become green then because the Croats who weren't killed were expelled. But here we're looking at the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, to make sure that no one makes a mistake, we should look at this map on a daily basis to see who attacks, who takes control, who kills, who occupies what village, who leaves, to have a clear picture. When you worked for the Intelligence Service, how could you follow everything by the minute, as the events were unfolding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had a large map, a very large map, and we placed a foil on top of it. And it was on this foil -- well, you could draw on it. You could use the felt-tipped pens to write across this foil, and then you could rub them out, rub the changes out by using alcohol, and make new entries. And that's the kind of map that we kept for the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would still like to talk about Trusina. When did you hear that there had been killings in Trusina? This is something I discover on the map, and it's the first time I hear about the fact that you were using a map with a trace paper. In Zerka [as interpreted], you changed the positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, we did use those maps, and we would draw in the positions when individual places fell mostly, and we learnt about their fall from the refugees coming in and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the small village of Glace [as interpreted]. It is at the bottom to the right-hand side. It is surrounded by Muslims. I assume that at the time the ABiH must have occupied this village, and what we see in blue here must have turned to green very quickly. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's the village of Cerici. It was -- or Gerici. I don't know whether it's a G or a C. What is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So just in follow-up to one of the responses that you gave earlier regarding -- that the villages with Croat populations, that the intention was to include them with regard to military matters in the HZ-HB, is that how I understood you?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question properly, or perhaps it's a question of interpretation or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure that in more than one element it quite accurately reflects what the witness said, whether Mr. Kruger is intending to use the witness's specific answer or follow-up in a general sense. But if he's saying that he gets the elements of that question from the witness's previous responses, could we know exactly where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'll just rephrase the question. I don't have the transcript open in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You recall, sir, that we referred to the two villages of Pozetva and Buscak, and I asked you, Does that mean that these two villages with Croat populations were intended to be included within the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Could you just repeat your response to that, that I can just understand it, please?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're now talking about territory. The Croatian Community, to the best of my knowledge, did not have a compact territory. It was organised to help all the Croats where they were in the majority in the villages, and everybody else who wanted to become involved in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But what about those two villages? Does that mean that the HVO wanted to establish its administration in those villages over Croats?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Croatian Defence Council is concerned for Konjic, the Croatian Defence Council had, in the area sometime in May 1993, one brigade. Now, that brigade was composed of three battalions. That means that the people from these villages were involved in those battalions, included in them, and holding the lines facing the Army of Republika Srpska. So one battalion was in the area of Konjic town, the other one was in Neretvica, and the third one was Jablanica. So it was organised -- the brigade was organised to defend the population against the Army of Republika Srpska, and in the brigade you had taking part people from all these villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, unless I'm mistaken - I may make a mistake - you have said that the ABiH and the HVO faced the VRS. When I look at these Serb villages, there are not very many of them, and without knowing those exact locations, in military terms, all these small localities could fall very easily. And in Konjic, the Serb issue was not a major issue because Bijela, Borci, all these small villages, well, weren't facing the artillery or Serb tanks. So this is my question: In this municipality of Konjic, did the Serb pose a major threat to the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not in the town, itself, because a large portion of the Serbs had left town, those who had joined up with the Army of Republika Srpska. And those who stayed on in the town were considered to be ordinary citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and neither the HVO nor the BH Army thought them to be enemies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, Colonel, in 1993 where were the Serbs or the VRS? Were they in Bradina, were they in Bircani, in Zabrdje, in Bijela? Were there Serb forces there or not? Because you see, Colonel, the problem that we have in this trial -- please wait. Just listen to me first. The Judges do not have all the documents. If we had the documents of the Main Staff of the HVO, as well as of the ABiH, as well as of the Serbs, we would have an overall vision of the situation, but we are given what the Prosecutor and what the Defence is ready to give us. And here I see Serb villages, and I don't really know whether the VRS was there, whether there were Serb tanks there. I don't know. Because you were in charge of military intelligence, so I'm wondering whether the VRS was positioned in those villages. That's the question I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything was to the east of Konjic, including Borci, south of Konjic. That's where the Army of Republika Srpska was. Now, this isn't a topographical map, but I do know the village of Borci. They were not in Bradina, for example, but they were close to Bradina. Bijela, Borci, and further on upwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really do consider the question that you've just raised to be a very important one and that a complete answer to that question cannot be given if you only look at Konjic municipality. So if we take a look at the previous map, which is document P9276, then we'll have a clearer and fuller picture and we'll see what the surrounding parts are around Konjic municipality that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska and could be important for the BH Army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We'll take that on board. Thank you, Colonel. You said that according to you, the VRS was in Borci, in Zagorici [phoen], so you confirm that they were there. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bijela, Borci, and further up towards Bradina, but not Bradina itself. Towards Bjelasnica here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's very useful for us to understand. Mr. Kruger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just before showing you a video: Apart from -- apart from the HVO military situation, isn't it correct that the HVO civilian authorities weren't interested in the red dots; they wanted to establish control over entire municipalities? What would you say to that if I put that to you?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that any attempts were made to establish civilian authority in a municipality where the Croats weren't in a majority, that is to say, that they would have full authority over the entire region or over the whole of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have an objection to the question, but if you allow me to say this: I think that Mr. Kruger has started broaching the subject about civilian authorities, which wasn't raised during the examination-in-chief. He has the right to do so, of course. But according to your guide-lines, in that case Mr. Kruger does not have the right to pose leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. Kruger, according to our guide-lines, when the topic was not touched upon during the examination-in-chief, you have to ask neutral questions and not leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what the HVO -- what the HVO civilian authorities felt with regard to the establishment of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, as far as the civilian structures are concerned within the HVO, the aim was to organise life and work in the areas which were populated by a Croatian majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you were an intelligence analyst, and obviously you said you were receiving intelligence reports regarding the activities of the ABiH. What was the ABiH's view about what the HVO was trying to establish in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean. What do you mean, what the HVO was trying to establish in Konjic? The HVO in Konjic had a brigade which, together with the BH Army, took part to a large extent in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in defending it from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Didn't you receive information that the ABiH was concerned that the HVO wanted to take the whole of Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody had any information to send out of that kind because the Croatian Defence Council in the Konjic area had about 1.250 soldiers, while during that same period the BH Army numbered between 14.000 and 17.000 soldiers, depending on which period we look at. Therefore, I don't know which army would be afraid of somebody who is -- who has so much fewer men and not better armed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the town of Mostar was being claimed as the capital of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the Croatian Community saw Mostar as somewhere where the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had his headquarters, without any special rights, any other rights, because, as some people used to say, that was the only town which in that area had traffic lights or a set of traffic lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, we have a few moments left, and let's change the pace and let's have a look at a video-clip. And I'm referring to Exhibit P02187, and I'm going to show you a clip of a meeting between General Halilovic and General Petkovic. And this was, I think, on the 4th of May, 1993. Now, I'm only going to show you two portions of this and then ask you a few questions which will lead on into our next topic, which we'll probably deal with tomorrow. So the first part I'm going to show you is where General Halilovic is speaking, and this is about five minutes into the tape at 5 minutes, 27 seconds. If we can have a look at the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, is there translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, we have no sound. Could we perhaps start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems we have a problem, and perhaps it's best to start tomorrow morning with this tape. It seems we have no sound. We can follow the English, but it seems the witness cannot follow the sound then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Nothing. Your Honour, if we can terminate the videotape now, and I'll just do a short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, we'll look at this video again tomorrow. Just perhaps before we do that: Did you recognise any of the footage there? Were you present at that particular meeting or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, I wasn't present at that meeting, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's look very quickly at Exhibit P00195. It's the first document in the binder, and this is a document dated 8 May 1992, by Colonel General Ante Roso. And it says: "On the basis of the --" It says: "On the basis of the previous agreements and existing needs, I issue the following order:" And he says: "The only legal military units in the territory of the HZ-HB are units of the HVO. All other military units in the above territory must join the single defence system and recognise the HVO Main Staff as their supreme command." So, sir, if I understand correctly, "military units on the territory of the HZ-HB," that would mean the municipalities which are included in the decree which decreed the existence or into existence the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that, and I don't know who this was sent to at all, and what this is all about, and what the role was of General Roso there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kruger. I do not see in the original a word like "territory," but I think it's "pastrojbe," but I'm not quite sure. Perhaps if the witness would read number 1, we will hear how the translators would -- the interpreters would render this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, could you please read -- could you please read point number 1 of this record?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the territory of the HZ-HB," "prostor," "the only legal military units are the 'postrojbe' HVO." So it seems to be "postrojbe" and not -- I can't see the end of that word to know which word it is exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but we're coming back to our old topic, and I'd like to ask the interpreters to avoid -- I'd like to ask the interpreters to translate the word "prostor" as "area" and not "territory." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, whether it's "area" or "territory," my question does remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, where would this leave the municipality of Konjic? Would only the HVO be the legal military organisation for the area on the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I don't know in what role General Roso was signing this and to whom it is addressed, so we can't see who this is addressed to. And I don't know what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can look at one further document before the break, it will be very quick. If you look at the very next document in your binder -- well, first, before turning there, you see that the confidential number or the reference number at the top of your document is "01-331-92." Now turn to the next document, P00200, and this is an order by Tihomir Blaskic on the 11th of May, 1992, and we'll see that on the basis of the orders received from the main headquarters, confidential number, and we have the same reference number, "01-331/92" of 8 May: "I order," and then he says: "The only legal military units in the area of Kiseljak municipality are HVO units."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So you see that General Roso's order was being implemented. You agree?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can see that on the basis of this order, something was written, but I think that at the time nothing existed, except for the HVO, on the territory of Kiseljak, in the area of Kiseljak, because if we were to show the ethnic map like we did for Konjic, then you would be able to see that the Croats are in the majority there and that they organised themselves -- that they were the only ones that were organised and that nothing else existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if perhaps that is the appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed you're right. It is 7.00 p.m. We'll have a break of a few hours. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry for the interruption, and greetings to you and the Chamber. Just to follow up on the videotape that we had the technical problems with. The Trial Chamber might recall that we tried and failed about three or four times to run some video-clips in this courtroom early during the cross-examination of General Praljak, and it caused a tremendous amount of inconvenience to the Prosecution which we were only able to fix by delaying the videotapes until after the summer recess when we were back in Courtroom III, where the system seems to work better. We're no going to have that luxury here, and so just because we have the short turnaround and because we're back in the courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00, I'd just like to express our gratitude for the technical people to make sure that this technical problem is fixed and that the videotapes are working properly first thing in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As Mr. Stringer said, we are going to resume in this courtroom at 9.00, and let's hope that the technicians have solved the problem before then. I wish you a good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
